**Ch 007 draft — screening pass**

**"The only idea which would have been quite unreasonable scarcely entered his mind. This was the thought of going westward and growing up with the country."**

In the source, this paragraph opens with a full logical setup: the ideas (feeling himself somewhere else, Europe, Washington) were *more than reasonable* — they were the logical, necessary, mathematical result of conditions. *Only* the idea of going westward would have been unreasonable. The draft cuts the entire "Had these ideas been unreasonable… more than reasonable; they were the logical, necessary, mathematical result…" bridge. So the sentence "The only idea which would have been quite unreasonable scarcely entered his mind" lands as a broken pivot: it is the second side of a contrast ("all those ideas were reasonable; *only* this one was not"), but the first side — the explicit statement that the other ideas were reasonable/logical — was cut. A reader encountering "The only idea which would have been quite unreasonable" has no preceding referent for what the contrasted (reasonable) ideas are, since the draft's preceding paragraph simply describes watching Cunard steamers, without any evaluative framing establishing those feelings as "more than reasonable." The "only" creates a superlative contrast against a set that has not been declared or evaluated in the draft.

Gate test: A competent reader would genuinely wonder what body of ideas is being implicitly praised as reasonable, since the draft never sets up the evaluative frame. They are not merely reading a less-ornamented version; the logical hinge is missing.
